items.stem: Which species contains a coordination bond?
items.answer: NH₄⁺
items.markingKey: C. N lone pair donated to H⁺.

items.stem: Which species has a central atom with only six valence electrons?
items.answer: BCl₃
items.markingKey: D. B: 3 bonding pairs, no lone pairs.

items.stem: Explain how a coordination bond forms in the oxonium ion, H₃O⁺.
items.answer: A lone pair on the oxygen of H₂O is donated into the empty orbital of an H⁺ ion; once formed, the coordination bond is identical to the other O–H bonds.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A lone pair on the oxygen of H₂O is donated into the empty orbital of an H⁺ ion; once formed, the coordination bond is identical to the other O–H bonds. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: How many bonding pairs and lone pairs of electrons are in the Lewis formula of N₂?
items.answer: 3 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs
items.markingKey: B. N₂: 3 shared pairs and 2 non-bonding pairs.

items.stem: Which of the following contains a coordination (dative covalent) bond: CH₃OH, H₃O⁺, HCl and NH₃?
items.answer: H₃O⁺
items.markingKey: A. In H₃O⁺ one atom supplies both electrons of a shared pair (e.g. N or O lone pair → H⁺, O → C in CO, N → B in H₃N–BF₃, Cl → Al in Al₂Cl₆).

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Lewis formulae are an adequate model of bonding in molecules."
items.answer: A powerful first model whose limitations are addressed by resonance and orbital (σ/π, hybridisation) models.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: predict bonding and lone pairs, used for VSEPR shapes; explain octets and coordination bonds. Arguments against: cannot represent resonance/delocalisation with a single structure; say nothing about orbitals, bond energies or magnetism (O₂ is paramagnetic); fail for electron-deficient species. Supported judgement: A powerful first model whose limitations are addressed by resonance and orbital (σ/π, hybridisation) models.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "bond length".
items.answer: The average distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the average distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain how a coordination bond forms in [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺.
items.answer: Each water oxygen donates a lone pair to Cu²⁺ (six coordination bonds).
items.markingKey: each water oxygen donates a lone pair to Cu²⁺ (six coordination bonds) (1); both electrons of the shared pair come from the donor atom (1).

items.stem: Chloé writes: "A double bond is twice as strong as a single bond." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: A C=C bond (614 kJ mol⁻¹) is less than twice a C–C bond (346 kJ mol⁻¹) because the second (π) bond is weaker than the σ bond.
items.markingKey: A C=C bond (614 kJ mol⁻¹) is less than twice a C–C bond (346 kJ mol⁻¹) because the second (π) bond is weaker than the σ bond. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: How many valence electrons in total must be shown in the Lewis formula of the NO₃⁻ ion?
items.markingKey: B. 1 × 5 (N) + 3 × 6 (O) + 1 (charge) = 24 electrons (12 pairs).

items.stem: Hydrazine, N₂H₄, is used as a rocket fuel. (a) Draw its Lewis formula. (b) State the number of bonding pairs and lone pairs. (c) Predict the H–N–H bond angle and explain it. (d) Explain why hydrazine is a liquid at room temperature while ethane (similar Mr) is a gas.
items.answer: (a) H₂N–NH₂ with one lone pair on each N. (b) 5 bonding pairs, 2 lone pairs. (c) about 107°: four electron domains (tetrahedral), lone pair repels more strongly. (d) hydrazine forms hydrogen bonds (N–H…N); ethane has only London forces.
items.markingKey: (a) H₂N–NH₂ with one lone pair on each N. (b) 5 bonding pairs, 2 lone pairs. (c) about 107°: four electron domains (tetrahedral), lone pair repels more strongly. (d) hydrazine forms hydrogen bonds (N–H…N); ethane has only London forces.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "molecular geometry".
items.answer: The arrangement of the atoms in a molecule, determined by the positions of the bonding domains only
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the arrangement of the atoms in a molecule, determined by the positions of the bonding domains only. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which molecule has the smallest bond angle?
items.answer: H₂O
items.markingKey: D. Two lone pairs: 104.5°.

items.stem: Explain why the bond angle in ammonia (107°) is less than that in methane (109.5°).
items.answer: Both have four electron domains in a tetrahedral arrangement, but in NH₃ one is a lone pair; lone pairs are closer to the nucleus and repel bonding pairs more strongly, pushing the N–H bonds closer together.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Both have four electron domains in a tetrahedral arrangement, but in NH₃ one is a lone pair; lone pairs are closer to the nucleus and repel bonding pairs more strongly, pushing the N–H bonds closer together. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: What is the molecular geometry of OF₂?
items.answer: bent (V-shaped)
items.markingKey: A. 4 domains (2 lone pairs) → bent (V-shaped).

items.stem: "A double bond counts as two electron domains." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: A double bond is one electron domain; e.g. CO₂ has two domains and is linear.
items.markingKey: A double bond is one electron domain; e.g. CO₂ has two domains and is linear. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: State the number of electron domains around the central atom in CCl₄ and the molecule's shape.
items.answer: 4; tetrahedral
items.markingKey: 4 (1); tetrahedral (1).

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "VSEPR theory reliably predicts the shapes of all molecules."
items.answer: VSEPR is an excellent predictive tool for main-group shapes but is approximate and has limited scope.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: correct for most main-group molecules; simple to apply from Lewis formulae; explains bond-angle reductions due to lone pairs. Arguments against: does not give exact angles (e.g. H₂S 92°); less reliable for transition metal complexes; treats domains qualitatively; orbital models are needed for bonding energies. Supported judgement: VSEPR is an excellent predictive tool for main-group shapes but is approximate and has limited scope.

items.stem: Compare the shapes and bond angles of NCl₃ and CH₄. In your answer (a) state the number of bonding and non-bonding domains on each central atom, (b) deduce each molecular geometry and bond angle, and (c) explain the difference in bond angle.
items.answer: NCl₃: 3 bonding, 1 lone; trigonal pyramidal, about 107°. CH₄: 4 bonding, 0 lone; tetrahedral, 109.5°.
items.markingKey: (a) domain counts for both (A1 A1). (b) geometries and angles (A1 A1). (c) different numbers of domains and/or lone pairs; lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs, compressing angles (R1).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "electron domain"?
options: The tendency of a substance to vaporise; volatile substances have weak intermolecular forces and low boiling points
A region of electron density around a central atom: a lone pair, a single bond or a multiple bond each count as one domain
The relative ability of an atom to attract a shared pair of electrons in a covalent bond
A covalent bond formed by the sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals, with electron density above and below the internuclear axis
items.answer: A region of electron density around a central atom: a lone pair, a single bond or a multiple bond each count as one domain
items.markingKey: B. "electron domain" is a region of electron density around a central atom: a lone pair, a single bond or a multiple bond each count as one domain.

items.stem: Which pair has the same molecular geometry?
items.answer: NH₃ and PCl₃
items.markingKey: B. Both trigonal pyramidal.

items.stem: Explain the difference between molecular geometry and electron domain geometry.
items.answer: Electron domain geometry includes all domains (bonds and lone pairs); molecular geometry describes only the positions of the atoms – they differ when lone pairs are present (e.g. NH₃: tetrahedral vs trigonal pyramidal).
items.markingKey: Electron domain geometry includes all domains (bonds and lone pairs); molecular geometry describes only the positions of the atoms – they differ when lone pairs are present (e.g. NH₃: tetrahedral vs trigonal pyramidal). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Water is linear because it has only two bonds." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Water has four electron domains (two bonds, two lone pairs) in a tetrahedral arrangement; the molecule is bent (104.5°).
items.markingKey: Water has four electron domains (two bonds, two lone pairs) in a tetrahedral arrangement; the molecule is bent (104.5°). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: What is the molecular geometry of NO₂⁻?
items.answer: bent (V-shaped)
items.markingKey: A. 3 domains (1 lone pairs) → bent (V-shaped).

items.stem: Compare the shapes and bond angles of CCl₄ and NCl₃. In your answer (a) state the number of bonding and non-bonding domains on each central atom, (b) deduce each molecular geometry and bond angle, and (c) explain the difference in bond angle.
items.answer: CCl₄: 4 bonding, 0 lone; tetrahedral, 109.5°. NCl₃: 3 bonding, 1 lone; trigonal pyramidal, about 107°.
items.markingKey: (a) domain counts for both (A1 A1). (b) geometries and angles (A1 A1). (c) different numbers of domains and/or lone pairs; lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs, compressing angles (R1).

items.stem: Define the term "bond dipole".
items.answer: The separation of partial charges along a polar bond, shown with an arrow pointing towards the more electronegative atom
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the separation of partial charges along a polar bond, shown with an arrow pointing towards the more electronegative atom. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Leila writes: "In a C–Cl bond the carbon atom carries a partial negative charge." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Chlorine (3.2) is more electronegative than carbon (2.6), so Cl is δ− and C is δ+.
items.markingKey: Chlorine (3.2) is more electronegative than carbon (2.6), so Cl is δ− and C is δ+. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A charged rod deflects a stream of liquid. Which liquid is it most likely to be?
items.answer: water
items.markingKey: C. Polar molecules are attracted to the rod.

items.stem: Which of the molecules BrF₅, C₂H₄, H₂O and OF₂ is non-polar?
items.answer: C₂H₄
items.markingKey: B. C₂H₄ is trigonal planar; its bond dipoles cancel by symmetry (or the bonds are non-polar).

items.stem: Calculate the electronegativity difference for the C–F bond and indicate the bond dipole.
items.answer: ΔEN = |2.6 − 4.0| = 1.4; F is δ−, C is δ+; polar covalent.
items.markingKey: ΔEN = 1.4 (1); δ− on F (more electronegative) (1); polar covalent (1).

items.stem: PCl₃ and BF₃ both contain polar bonds. (a) Deduce the shape of each molecule. (b) Explain which molecule is polar. (c) Predict which liquid would be deflected by a charged rod and which would be more soluble in water, giving reasons.
items.answer: (a) PCl₃ trigonal pyramidal, BF₃ trigonal planar; (b) PCl₃ polar; (c) PCl₃ deflected and more soluble in water
items.markingKey: (a) shapes (A1 A1). (b) PCl₃: trigonal pyramidal – dipoles do not cancel; BF₃: trigonal planar – dipoles cancel (R1). (c) polar PCl₃ is attracted to the charged rod (R1); polar molecules interact with polar water (dipole–dipole/H-bonds) (R1).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A covalent bond in which the electrons are shared unequally because the atoms differ in electronegativity, giving partial charges δ+ and δ−"?
items.answer: polar covalent bond
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of polar covalent bond.

items.stem: Explain whether OF₂ is a polar or a non-polar molecule.
items.answer: Polar: the bonds are polar, and the bent (V-shaped) shape means the bond dipoles do not cancel.
items.markingKey: Bonds are polar (electronegativity difference) (1); shape bent (V-shaped) (1); dipoles do not cancel – polar (1).

items.stem: What is the electronegativity difference for the H–I bond, and which atom carries the partial negative charge?
options: 0.9, with the δ− end on I
4.9, with the δ− end on I
0.5, with the δ− end on H
0.5, with the δ− end on I
items.answer: 0.5, with the δ− end on I
items.markingKey: D. EN(H) = 2.2, EN(I) = 2.7; ΔEN = 0.5; the more electronegative atom (I) is δ−.

items.stem: Which molecule is polar?
items.answer: PCl₃
items.markingKey: B. PCl₃ is trigonal pyramidal; bond dipoles do not cancel.

items.stem: "The Pauling electronegativity scale is an objective measurement." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: It is a useful but constructed quantity; its numbers are model-dependent rather than directly measured.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: values are derived from measured bond enthalpies; consistent and widely used. Arguments against: electronegativity cannot be measured directly – it is a derived, relative concept; other scales (Mulliken, Allred–Rochow) give different values; values depend on oxidation state and hybridisation. Supported judgement: It is a useful but constructed quantity; its numbers are model-dependent rather than directly measured. Markbands (12 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "intermolecular forces"?
options: A covalent bond in which the electrons are shared unequally because the atoms differ in electronegativity, giving partial charges δ+ and δ−
The tendency of a substance to vaporise; volatile substances have weak intermolecular forces and low boiling points
A pair of valence electrons on an atom that is not involved in bonding
The attractive forces between molecules (London dispersion, dipole–dipole and hydrogen bonding), much weaker than covalent bonds
items.answer: The attractive forces between molecules (London dispersion, dipole–dipole and hydrogen bonding), much weaker than covalent bonds
items.markingKey: D. "intermolecular forces" is the attractive forces between molecules (London dispersion, dipole–dipole and hydrogen bonding), much weaker than covalent bonds.

items.stem: "Hydrogen bonds form between any molecules containing hydrogen." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Hydrogen bonding requires H covalently bonded to N, O or F; e.g. CH₄ cannot hydrogen-bond.
items.markingKey: Hydrogen bonding requires H covalently bonded to N, O or F; e.g. CH₄ cannot hydrogen-bond. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Which statement about London dispersion forces is correct?
options: They are stronger than hydrogen bonds in small molecules.
They exist only between polar molecules.
They increase as the number of electrons increases.
items.answer: They increase as the number of electrons increases.
items.markingKey: D. More polarisable electron cloud.

items.stem: What is the strongest type of intermolecular force between molecules of H₂O?
items.answer: hydrogen bonding
items.markingKey: A. H₂O: hydrogen bonding (and London forces).

items.stem: Which substance has the highest boiling point?
items.answer: stibine
items.markingKey: C. phosphine −88 °C, ammonia −33 °C, arsine −62 °C, stibine −17 °C.

items.stem: Which substance forms hydrogen bonds between its own molecules: CHCl₃, CO₂, H₂O and HCl?
items.answer: H₂O
items.markingKey: C. Hydrogen bonding between identical molecules needs H bonded directly to N, O or F and a lone pair on N, O or F. H₂O has O–H bonds.

items.stem: Explain the following in terms of intermolecular forces: (a) iodine is a solid at room temperature while chlorine is a gas; (b) ice floats on water; (c) propanone mixes with water although it cannot hydrogen-bond to itself.
items.answer: (a) I₂ has many more electrons (106 vs 34) – much stronger London forces. (b) hydrogen-bonded open lattice in ice is less dense. (c) the C=O oxygen lone pairs accept hydrogen bonds from water molecules; dipole–dipole interactions also help.
items.markingKey: (a) I₂ has many more electrons (106 vs 34) – much stronger London forces. (b) hydrogen-bonded open lattice in ice is less dense. (c) the C=O oxygen lone pairs accept hydrogen bonds from water molecules; dipole–dipole interactions also help.

items.stem: Ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH) boils at 118 °C and propan-1-ol (C₃H₇OH) at 97 °C. (a) Identify all the intermolecular forces present in each substance. (b) Explain the difference in boiling points. (c) Suggest which substance has the higher enthalpy of vaporisation and why.
items.answer: (b) both H-bond, but ethanoic acid forms hydrogen-bonded dimers and has more H-bonding sites; (c) ethanoic acid
items.markingKey: (a) forces in each correctly identified (A1 A1). (b) both H-bond, but ethanoic acid forms hydrogen-bonded dimers and has more H-bonding sites (R1 R1). (c) ethanoic acid: stronger intermolecular forces need more energy to separate the molecules (R1).

items.stem: Briefly explain why hydrogen fluoride has a higher boiling point than hydrogen chloride.
items.answer: HF molecules form strong hydrogen bonds (H bonded to highly electronegative F with small size and lone pairs); HCl has only dipole–dipole and London forces.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: HF molecules form strong hydrogen bonds (H bonded to highly electronegative F with small size and lone pairs); HCl has only dipole–dipole and London forces. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between hydrogen bonds and London forces.
items.answer: London forces arise from temporary dipoles and exist between all molecules; hydrogen bonds are stronger attractions requiring H bonded to N, O or F and a lone pair on N, O or F of another molecule.
items.markingKey: London forces arise from temporary dipoles and exist between all molecules; hydrogen bonds are stronger attractions requiring H bonded to N, O or F and a lone pair on N, O or F of another molecule. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between intermolecular forces and intramolecular (covalent) bonds.
items.answer: Intermolecular forces act between separate molecules and are weak; covalent bonds hold the atoms within a molecule together and are much stronger.
items.markingKey: Intermolecular forces act between separate molecules and are weak; covalent bonds hold the atoms within a molecule together and are much stronger. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Predict, with reasons, the order of boiling points (lowest first) of: iodine (I₂), fluorine (F₂), bromine (Br₂), chlorine (Cl₂).
items.markingKey: Correct order F₂ < Cl₂ < Br₂ < I₂ (b.p. −188 °C, −34 °C, 59 °C, 184 °C) (1); London forces increase with number of electrons / surface area (1).

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Hydrogen bonding is the most important intermolecular force."
items.answer: Hydrogen bonds are the strongest per interaction, but for many large molecules London forces contribute more overall – the importance is context dependent.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: explains the anomalous properties of water, HF, NH₃; essential for DNA base pairing and protein structure. Arguments against: London forces dominate in large molecules (waxes, polymers, iodine); London forces are present in all molecules and often contribute most of the total attraction; importance depends on the substance. Supported judgement: Hydrogen bonds are the strongest per interaction, but for many large molecules London forces contribute more overall – the importance is context dependent. Markbands (6 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem:
The boiling points of some hydrides are shown.

hydride | boiling point / °C
H₂O | 100
H₂S | −60
H₂Se | −41
H₂Te | −2

(a) Describe and explain the trend from the second to the last hydride. (b) Explain why H₂O does not follow this trend. (c) Predict, with a reason, the boiling point H₂O would have if it followed the trend.
items.answer: (a) increases: more electrons, stronger London forces; (b) hydrogen bonding in H₂O; (c) below the second hydride (extrapolated, roughly −80 to −100 °C)
items.markingKey: (a) b.p. increases down the group (A1); molecules have more electrons/larger, so stronger London forces (R1). (b) H₂O forms hydrogen bonds – H bonded to a small, highly electronegative atom with lone pairs (R1); much more energy to separate (R1). (c) extrapolation gives a value lower than H₂S (R1).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A giant structure in which atoms are joined by covalent bonds throughout, e.g. diamond, graphite and silicon dioxide"?
items.answer: covalent network structure
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of covalent network structure.

items.stem: Briefly explain why π bonds are weaker than σ bonds.
items.answer: Sideways overlap of p orbitals is less effective than head-on overlap, so the electron density between the nuclei is lower.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Sideways overlap of p orbitals is less effective than head-on overlap, so the electron density between the nuclei is lower. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Silicon dioxide has a low melting point because it is made of small SiO₂ molecules like CO₂." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: SiO₂ is a covalent network (each Si bonded to four O); many strong Si–O bonds must break, so its melting point is about 1700 °C.
items.markingKey: SiO₂ is a covalent network (each Si bonded to four O); many strong Si–O bonds must break, so its melting point is about 1700 °C. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: What is the hybridisation of the central C atom in CO₃²⁻?
items.answer: sp²
items.markingKey: A. 3 electron domains → sp².

items.stem: How many sigma (σ) and pi (π) bonds are present in one molecule of propene?
items.answer: 8 σ and 1 π
items.markingKey: B. CH₂=CHCH₃: each single bond is σ; a double bond is σ + π; a triple bond is σ + 2π. Total 8 σ, 1 π.

items.stem: For propenenitrile, CH₂=CHCN: (a) state the number of σ and π bonds; (b) deduce the hybridisation of each carbon atom; (c) explain how a π bond forms; (d) predict the bond angle(s) around the carbon atoms.
items.answer: (a) 6 σ, 3 π; (b) C=C carbons sp²; C≡N carbon sp; (d) 120°, 180°
items.markingKey: (a) 6 σ, 3 π (A1 A1). (b) C=C carbons sp²; C≡N carbon sp (A1). (c) sideways overlap of unhybridised p orbitals above and below the σ bond axis (R1). (d) 120°, 180° (A1).

items.stem: What is the hybridisation of the carbon atom in CO₂?
items.answer: sp
items.markingKey: A. Two electron domains.

items.stem: Which statement explains the very high melting point of diamond?
options: Many strong covalent bonds must be broken.
items.answer: Many strong covalent bonds must be broken.
items.markingKey: C. Covalent network.

items.stem: State the numbers of sigma and pi bonds in ethanal.
items.answer: 6 σ, 1 π
items.markingKey: Every single bond is one σ; a double bond is 1σ + 1π; a triple bond 1σ + 2π: 6 σ (1) and 1 π (1).

items.stem: Which describes the hybridisation of the central atom and the molecular geometry of CO₃²⁻?
items.answer: sp² and trigonal planar
items.markingKey: A. 3 electron domains (0 lone pairs) → sp²; geometry trigonal planar.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The arrangement of all electron domains (bonding and non-bonding) around a central atom"?
items.answer: electron domain geometry
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of electron domain geometry.

items.stem: Why does water have a much higher boiling point than hydrogen sulfide?
items.answer: Water molecules form hydrogen bonds.
items.markingKey: C. H₂S has only weak dipole–dipole and London forces.

items.stem: Which molecule contains a triple bond?
items.answer: N₂
items.markingKey: N₂. N≡N.

items.stem: Distinguish between a polar molecule and a polar bond.
items.answer: A polar bond has unequal sharing of electrons between two atoms; a polar molecule has a net dipole, which requires polar bonds arranged unsymmetrically.
items.markingKey: A polar bond has unequal sharing of electrons between two atoms; a polar molecule has a net dipole, which requires polar bonds arranged unsymmetrically. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between diamond and graphite.
items.answer: Diamond: each C sp³, four bonds, 3D tetrahedral network, hard, non-conductor; graphite: each C sp², three bonds in hexagonal layers with delocalised electrons, soft, conducts.
items.markingKey: Diamond: each C sp³, four bonds, 3D tetrahedral network, hard, non-conductor; graphite: each C sp², three bonds in hexagonal layers with delocalised electrons, soft, conducts. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between molecular geometry and electron domain geometry.
items.answer: Electron domain geometry includes all domains (bonds and lone pairs); molecular geometry describes only the positions of the atoms – they differ when lone pairs are present (e.g. NH₃: tetrahedral vs trigonal pyramidal).
items.markingKey: Electron domain geometry includes all domains (bonds and lone pairs); molecular geometry describes only the positions of the atoms – they differ when lone pairs are present (e.g. NH₃: tetrahedral vs trigonal pyramidal). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Which molecule can form hydrogen bonds with water but not with itself?
items.answer: propanone, CH₃COCH₃
items.markingKey: D. C=O lone pairs accept H-bonds; no O–H or N–H to donate.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a bonding pair and a lone pair.
items.answer: A bonding pair is shared between two atoms; a lone pair belongs to one atom and is not used in bonding.
items.markingKey: A bonding pair is shared between two atoms; a lone pair belongs to one atom and is not used in bonding. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why electronegativity increases across period 3.
items.answer: Nuclear charge increases while electrons are added to the same shell, so shielding is similar; the atomic radius decreases and the bonding pair is attracted more strongly.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Nuclear charge increases while electrons are added to the same shell, so shielding is similar; the atomic radius decreases and the bonding pair is attracted more strongly. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Draw the resonance structures of benzene, C₆H₆ and deduce the average bond order.
items.answer: 2 equivalent resonance structures; bond order 1.5; electrons delocalised so all bonds identical.
items.markingKey: 2 resonance structures with double bond in different positions (1); delocalised π electrons over the bonds (1); bond order 1.5, intermediate length (1).

items.stem: Deduce the electron domain geometry and the molecular geometry of phosphorus trichloride, PCl₃, and predict its bond angle.
items.answer: electron domains 4 (tetrahedral); molecular geometry trigonal pyramidal; angle about 100° (less than 109.5°)
items.markingKey: 4 electron domains on P (3 bonding, 1 lone) (1); tetrahedral domain geometry (1); trigonal pyramidal, about 100° (less than 109.5°) (1).

items.stem: What is the strongest type of intermolecular force between molecules of NH₃ in the liquid state?
items.answer: hydrogen bonding
items.markingKey: C. NH₃: hydrogen bonding. Covalent bonds are intramolecular, not intermolecular.

items.stem: Which of CF₄, CO₂, NCl₃ and SF₆ has more than eight electrons in the valence shell of its central atom?
items.answer: SF₆
items.markingKey: D. SF₆ has an expanded octet (period 3+ central atom with more than four electron domains); the others obey the octet rule.

items.stem: Which bond is the least polar?
items.answer: C–Br
items.markingKey: D. Electronegativity differences: H–Cl 1.0, Na–Cl 2.3, C–Br 0.4, Al–Cl 1.6.

items.stem: Calculate the formal charge on each atom in the cyanide ion, [:C≡N:]⁻. (HL)
items.markingKey: FC = V − (L + ½B) applied to each atom (1); C −1, N 0 (1).

items.stem: A student claims: "A double bond counts as two electron domains." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: A double bond is one electron domain; e.g. CO₂ has two domains and is linear.
items.markingKey: A double bond is one electron domain; e.g. CO₂ has two domains and is linear. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Boiling point is a reliable indicator of the strength of intermolecular forces."
items.answer: Boiling point is a good indicator only when comparing similar molecular substances.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: higher b.p. reflects more energy needed to separate molecules; trends in homologous series are clear. Arguments against: b.p. also depends on molar mass, shape and entropy of vaporisation; comparisons are only fair between molecules of similar size; ionic and network solids have high b.p. due to bonds, not IMF. Supported judgement: Boiling point is a good indicator only when comparing similar molecular substances.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Lewis formulae are an adequate model of bonding in molecules."
items.answer: A powerful first model whose limitations are addressed by resonance and orbital (σ/π, hybridisation) models.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: predict bonding and lone pairs, used for VSEPR shapes; explain octets and coordination bonds. Arguments against: cannot represent resonance/delocalisation with a single structure; say nothing about orbitals, bond energies or magnetism (O₂ is paramagnetic); fail for electron-deficient species. Supported judgement: A powerful first model whose limitations are addressed by resonance and orbital (σ/π, hybridisation) models. Markbands (6 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: Using electronegativity values, (a) rank the bonds C–H, C–O, O–H and C–F in order of increasing polarity; (b) explain why methanol is polar; (c) explain why the C–F bond, though very polar, is very strong.
items.answer: (a) C–H (0.4) < C–O (0.8) < O–H (1.2) < C–F (1.4). (b) polar C–O and O–H bonds in a bent arrangement around O – dipoles do not cancel. (c) short bond with large ionic contribution adding to the covalent attraction (bond enthalpy 492 kJ mol⁻¹).
items.markingKey: (a) C–H (0.4) < C–O (0.8) < O–H (1.2) < C–F (1.4). (b) polar C–O and O–H bonds in a bent arrangement around O – dipoles do not cancel. (c) short bond with large ionic contribution adding to the covalent attraction (bond enthalpy 492 kJ mol⁻¹).

items.stem: "Hybridisation is a real physical process that occurs in atoms before they bond." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Hybridisation is a useful model consistent with molecular shapes but not a literal physical step – an illustration of the role of models in chemistry.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: explains equivalent bonds and observed geometries (e.g. CH₄); useful descriptive model linked to VSEPR. Arguments against: it is a mathematical model, not an observed process; molecular orbital theory explains some observations better (e.g. photoelectron spectra of CH₄). Supported judgement: Hybridisation is a useful model consistent with molecular shapes but not a literal physical step – an illustration of the role of models in chemistry. Markbands (12 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: What is the shape of a molecule with four bonding domains and no lone pairs on the central atom?
items.answer: tetrahedral
items.markingKey: C. Four domains as far apart as possible: 109.5°.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The attractive forces between molecules (London dispersion, dipole–dipole and hydrogen bonding), much weaker than covalent bonds"?
items.answer: intermolecular forces
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of intermolecular forces.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The tendency of atoms to gain, lose or share electrons until they have eight electrons in their outer (valence) shell"?
items.answer: octet rule
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of octet rule.

items.stem: Which molecule has polar bonds but is non-polar overall?
items.answer: BF₃
items.markingKey: C. Trigonal planar symmetry.

items.stem: Briefly explain why all the carbon–carbon bonds in benzene have the same length.
items.answer: Six π electrons are delocalised around the ring (resonance hybrid), so each C–C bond has a bond order of 1.5 and an intermediate length between single and double bonds.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Six π electrons are delocalised around the ring (resonance hybrid), so each C–C bond has a bond order of 1.5 and an intermediate length between single and double bonds. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why carbon dioxide is linear.
items.answer: The central carbon has two electron domains (two C=O double bonds) and no lone pairs; these repel to be as far apart as possible, at 180°.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The central carbon has two electron domains (two C=O double bonds) and no lone pairs; these repel to be as far apart as possible, at 180°. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Non-polar molecules have no intermolecular forces." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: All molecules experience London dispersion forces, which can be strong in large molecules (e.g. iodine is a solid).
items.markingKey: All molecules experience London dispersion forces, which can be strong in large molecules (e.g. iodine is a solid). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a lone pair and a bonding pair.
items.answer: A bonding pair is shared between two atoms; a lone pair belongs to one atom and is not used in bonding.
items.markingKey: A bonding pair is shared between two atoms; a lone pair belongs to one atom and is not used in bonding. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Deduce, with reference to its shape, whether ethene (C₂H₄) has a net dipole moment.
items.answer: Non-polar: the bonds are polar, and the trigonal planar shape means the bond dipoles cancel.
items.markingKey: Bonds are polar (electronegativity difference) (1); shape trigonal planar (1); dipoles cancel – non-polar (1).

items.stem: Explain, using resonance, why all the bonds in the ethanoate ion, CH₃COO⁻ are identical, and state the bond order.
items.answer: 2 equivalent resonance structures; bond order 1.5; electrons delocalised so all bonds identical.
items.markingKey: 2 resonance structures with double bond in different positions (1); delocalised π electrons over the bonds (1); bond order 1.5, intermediate length (1).

items.stem: Deduce the electron domain geometry and the molecular geometry of the nitrite ion, NO₂⁻, and predict its bond angle.
items.answer: electron domains 3 (trigonal planar); molecular geometry bent (V-shaped); angle about 115° (less than 120°)
items.markingKey: 3 electron domains on N (2 bonding, 1 lone) (1); trigonal planar domain geometry (1); bent (V-shaped), about 115° (less than 120°) (1).

items.stem: Predict, with reasons, the order of boiling points (lowest first) of: hydrogen chloride (HCl), hydrogen fluoride (HF), hydrogen bromide (HBr), hydrogen iodide (HI).
items.markingKey: Correct order HCl < HBr < HI < HF (b.p. −85 °C, −67 °C, −35 °C, 20 °C) (1); hydrogen bonding accounts for the anomalously high value(s) (1); London forces increase with number of electrons / surface area (1).

items.stem: Draw the Lewis formula of the nitrate ion (NO₃⁻) and state the number of bonding pairs and lone pairs it contains.
items.answer: 4 bonding pairs, 8 lone pairs
items.markingKey: Correct Lewis formula with all valence electrons (1); 4 bonding pairs (1); 8 lone pairs (1).

items.stem: Using electronegativity values from the data booklet, which of the bonds C–F, C–N, N–H and P–Cl is the least polar?
items.answer: C–N
items.markingKey: B. ΔEN: N–H 0.8, C–N 0.4, C–F 1.4, P–Cl 1.0. The larger the electronegativity difference, the more polar the bond.

items.stem: Deduce the number of σ and π bonds in a molecule of oxygen, O₂.
items.answer: 1 σ, 1 π
items.markingKey: Every single bond is one σ; a double bond is 1σ + 1π; a triple bond 1σ + 2π: 1 σ (1) and 1 π (1).

items.stem: What is the approximate bond angle in CH₄?
items.markingKey: C. tetrahedral: 109.5°.

items.stem:
The boiling points of some hydrides are shown.

hydride | boiling point / °C
HF | 20
HCl | −85
HBr | −67
HI | −35

(a) Describe and explain the trend from the second to the last hydride. (b) Explain why HF does not follow this trend. (c) Predict, with a reason, the boiling point HF would have if it followed the trend.
items.answer: (a) increases: more electrons, stronger London forces; (b) hydrogen bonding in HF; (c) below the second hydride (extrapolated, roughly −80 to −100 °C)
items.markingKey: (a) b.p. increases down the group (A1); molecules have more electrons/larger, so stronger London forces (R1). (b) HF forms hydrogen bonds – H bonded to a small, highly electronegative atom with lone pairs (R1); much more energy to separate (R1). (c) extrapolation gives a value lower than HCl (R1).

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Electronegativity values can be used to classify every bond sharply as ionic or covalent."
items.answer: Electronegativity difference indicates the degree of polarity/ionic character on a continuum rather than a strict classification.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: large differences (> 1.8) suggest ionic, small differences covalent; simple, data-booklet based. Arguments against: bonding is a continuum with no sharp boundary; values are relative and derived empirically; other factors (polarisation, structure) matter; e.g. HF has ΔEN 1.8 but is covalent. Supported judgement: Electronegativity difference indicates the degree of polarity/ionic character on a continuum rather than a strict classification. items.stem: For carbon dioxide, CO₂: (a) state the number of σ and π bonds; (b) deduce the hybridisation of each carbon atom; (c) explain how a π bond forms; (d) predict the bond angle(s) around the carbon atoms.
items.markingKey: (a) 2 σ, 2 π (A1 A1). (b) sp (A1). (c) sideways overlap of unhybridised p orbitals above and below the σ bond axis (R1). (d) 180° (A1).
